messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Conflict: Confrontations, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel is a 36-year-old tax consultant who came to treatment after months of pressure from his wife and a growing sense that his life had narrowed around rules he could no longer explain to himself. He had served in the military in his twenties, and when he speaks about the event that still governs his days, he does so in fragments. During a deployment, he was in a cramped interior space with other service members during a tense interaction that turned suddenly hostile. The moment that stays with him is not a clean narrative but a set of sharply preserved sensations: raised male voices, the split second when confrontation became unmistakably dangerous, the strange dead quiet just before it happened, and the taste in his mouth that returns to him even now with unnerving precision. He says that when the memory comes back he can taste it again as if he is there, a metallic, stale taste that seems to belong to fear and enclosed air and his own body bracing for what was about to happen.

In the months after he returned home, Daniel found that ordinary disagreement no longer felt ordinary. If a conversation became heated, or if someone pushed on a topic that felt too close to politics, war, military service, or anything resembling the arguments that had preceded the event, his whole body shifted. He did not describe this as remembering at first. He just knew that confrontations seemed charged in a way they had not before, and that certain conversation topics made him feel he needed to shut things down or get away. Even feeling physically unwell could set something off. If he was run-down, nauseated, feverish, or simply felt off in his body, he became less able to keep distance from what had happened; the memory would press closer, and with it the taste and the sense that he was no longer fully in the present.

At work, these patterns became woven into his routines. As a tax consultant, he spends much of the year in conference rooms with clients discussing money, mistakes, deadlines, and sometimes accusations. He has become the kind of man who scans every office before sitting down. He automatically notes the exits, where he could step out, what path would keep him from being boxed in. He cannot relax until he has mapped the room. If a client’s tone sharpens, if two people begin arguing over numbers, or if the room goes unusually quiet in the middle of a meeting, Daniel feels a hard surge of alarm. Silence is especially difficult for him; what unsettles him is the sense that when everything suddenly goes quiet, something dangerous is about to happen. His colleagues know him as controlled and prepared, but they have also noticed that he prefers to stand near doors and is unusually quick to end meetings that become tense.

At home, the effects have been more painful. Daniel is married, and one of the clearest changes has been around touch. If his wife comes up behind him and lays a hand on his shoulder, he startles violently before he can think. He hates the look on her face afterward, the hurt mixed with caution. He has tried to explain that unexpected contact hits him like an alarm, but he cannot bear prolonged discussion of the military event or what followed, so most conversations stop before either of them feels understood. He also pushes away moments that feel too good. A relaxed evening, affection, laughter, the warmth of feeling close to his wife—these have come to seem unsafe to him, as though letting himself feel positive emotion would leave him exposed. He pulls back from tenderness, changes the subject, gets busy, or goes quiet. Over time, his marriage has become organized around what not to do: don’t touch him unexpectedly, don’t ask too many questions, don’t linger on certain topics.

The memory itself is inconsistent in a way Daniel finds deeply unsettling. Sometimes when it returns, he is overwhelmed so quickly that he has to cut it off, stop talking, leave the room, or focus on anything else just to get through the next few minutes. At other times he can describe parts of it in a flat, detached way, as if it happened to someone else entirely. That emotional numbness frightens him almost as much as the overwhelming moments. He has come to believe that either he will be swallowed by the memory or he will disappear from it completely. Neither feels under his control.

What finally brought him in was not a single crisis but an accumulation. A client confrontation at work left him preoccupied with where the exits were and unable to settle for the rest of the day. Around the same time, he had been feeling physically unwell with a minor illness, and the old sensory fragments came back with unusual force. Then one evening his wife touched him unexpectedly in their kitchen and he recoiled so sharply that she began to cry. Daniel told the therapist he is tired of living as if every room needs an escape plan and every difficult conversation is edging toward danger. He is most afraid that this is simply who he is now—guarded, unreachable, impossible to comfort—but he is also hoping, carefully, that he might learn how to stay present without either shutting down or feeling overtaken.
